notes.front: What is remote identification (remote ID), in one sentence?
notes.back: The broadcast of an unmanned aircraft's identity, location and related data while it flies, as required by 14 CFR part 89.
notes.explanation: It gives the FAA, national security agencies and law enforcement awareness of who is flying where, to tell compliant users from possible risks.
notes.example: A receiver near a stadium picks up a passing drone's serial number and where its control station is.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.17.1; 14 CFR part 89
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: What is a standard remote identification unmanned aircraft, in one sentence?
notes.back: An unmanned aircraft built with remote identification that broadcasts its own and its control station's location from takeoff to shutdown.
notes.explanation: It is the first way to comply with remote ID, and needs no extra equipment from the pilot.
notes.example: A drone whose maker listed its serial number on an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance under part 89 and labelled it as meeting part 89.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: What is a remote identification broadcast module, in one sentence?
notes.back: A device fitted to an unmanned aircraft without built-in remote ID that broadcasts its identity, position and take-off location.
notes.explanation: It lets older drones comply with remote ID. It can be built in by the maker or be a standalone unit the user secures before takeoff.
notes.example: A pilot straps a small module, listed on an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance, to an older drone before flying.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.17.3.1; 14 CFR § 89.115(a)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: What is a FRIA, in one sentence?
notes.back: An FAA-recognized identification area: an approved site where unmanned aircraft without remote ID equipment may fly, within sight.
notes.explanation: It is the third way to comply with remote ID; only community-based organizations and educational institutions can apply for one.
notes.example: A university's approved flying field where students fly drones that have no broadcast equipment.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: What is GPS, in one sentence?
notes.back: The Global Positioning System: a satellite radio navigation and timing system operated by the U.S. Department of Defense.
notes.explanation: It tells an aircraft, or a drone carrying a GPS device, where it is.
notes.example: A drone’s GPS lets it hold its position in a hover.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16, “Global Positioning System”, p. 16-31; AC 107-2A ¶5.12.1

notes.front: What is air traffic control (ATC), in one sentence?
notes.back: The system of controllers whose main purpose is to prevent collisions between aircraft and to organise and speed the flow of traffic.
notes.explanation: This is why part 107 requires ATC authorization before a small drone flies in the airspace around many airports (§107.41).
notes.example: Like police directing traffic at a busy junction, but for aircraft: a controller tells each pilot where and when to go.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 15, “Air Traffic Control and the National Airspace System”, p. 15-7

notes.front: What is Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)?
notes.back: The single world time standard that aviation uses in place of local time, marked with a “Z” after the time.
notes.explanation: Times in reports are in UTC, not local time. Remote ID broadcasts carry a UTC time mark too (14 CFR § 89.305).
notes.example: A report time of 1845Z is 18:45 UTC.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 13, “Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)”

notes.front: What is ADS-B Out, in one sentence?
notes.back: Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast Out: equipment that transmits an aircraft's GPS position and other data to ground stations and nearby aircraft.
notes.explanation: It is a surveillance system for air traffic control and equipped aircraft; the drone rules keep part 107 aircraft off it.
notes.example: An airliner's ADS-B Out lets air traffic control and nearby equipped aircraft see where it is.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, p. 14-26; 14 CFR §§ 89.125, 107.53

notes.front: After {{c1::16 September 2023}}, no one may operate an unmanned aircraft in U.S. airspace unless the operation meets a remote ID requirement (§ 89.110 or § 89.115).
notes.explanation: The FAA can authorise otherwise, and aeronautical research flights have their own exception.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: What are the three ways a flight can meet the remote ID requirement?
notes.back: Fly a standard remote ID aircraft, fit a broadcast module, or fly within a FRIA.
notes.explanation: The first is § 89.110; the other two are the "alternative remote identification" options in § 89.115.
notes.source: 14 CFR §§ 89.105–89.115 (eCFR); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.17.3
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: A 0.5 lb drone will be flown under part 107. Must the flight meet remote ID?
notes.back: Yes. Part 107 requires registration, and remote ID applies to aircraft required to be registered, whatever their weight.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A notes that drones of 0.55 lb or less must still comply when flown under a part that requires registration.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.17.1; 14 CFR § 89.101
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: Your 2019 drone has no built-in remote ID. How can you fly it legally under part 107 today?
notes.back: Fit a broadcast module listed on an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance, or fly only within a FRIA.
notes.explanation: A drone without built-in remote ID is not a standard remote ID aircraft, so one of the two alternatives is needed. With a module, list the module’s serial number on the drone’s registration.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 89.115 (eCFR); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.17.3
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: When must a standard remote ID aircraft broadcast its remote ID message?
notes.back: From takeoff to shutdown.
notes.explanation: Its remote ID equipment must be working and not disabled throughout.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: What must the pilot do if a standard remote ID aircraft stops broadcasting during a flight?
notes.back: Land as soon as practicable.
notes.explanation: The duty falls on the person manipulating the flight controls. The same rule applies if a broadcast module stops.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: A pilot switches off remote ID on a standard remote ID aircraft, planning to keep it in sight all the time. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No. Its remote ID must be functional and not disabled from takeoff to shutdown.
notes.explanation: Keeping the aircraft in sight is a condition for broadcast modules and FRIAs, not a substitute for standard remote ID.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Mid-survey, your standard remote ID drone warns that it has stopped broadcasting. What do you do?
notes.back: Land as soon as practicable.
notes.choices:
A) Finish the survey, then land
B) Land as soon as practicable
C) Climb for a better signal and carry on
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: both continue the flight without the broadcast, which the rule does not allow.
notes.explanation: Remote ID must be broadcast from takeoff to shutdown; finishing the survey first would break that.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: For a standard remote ID aircraft, which serial number must be on its Certificate of Aircraft Registration?
notes.back: The aircraft's own serial number, assigned by its producer.
notes.explanation: It must also be listed on an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance (or be covered by a part 21 design or production approval).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: How does a standard remote ID aircraft identify itself in its broadcast?
notes.back: By its serial number or a session ID.
notes.explanation: It is one of eight minimum message elements; the rule allows a session ID as an alternative to the serial number.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Besides its own position, whose position does a standard remote ID aircraft broadcast?
notes.back: The control station's: its latitude, longitude and geometric altitude.
notes.explanation: The control station location must correspond to where the person manipulating the controls is.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Which three items describe the aircraft's own position in a standard remote ID broadcast?
notes.back: Its latitude, longitude and geometric altitude.
notes.explanation: The same three items are sent for the control station.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Besides identity and positions, which three items does a standard remote ID aircraft broadcast?
notes.back: Its velocity, a UTC time mark and its emergency status.
notes.explanation: That completes the eight minimum message elements of § 89.305.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: A remote ID receiver shows a drone's serial number, its position, its velocity, an emergency status and the pilot's position. Which kind of remote ID is it?
notes.back: A standard remote ID aircraft.
notes.explanation: Emergency status and the control station's position are broadcast only by standard remote ID; a broadcast module sends the take-off location instead.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: What identity does a broadcast module transmit?
notes.back: The module's own serial number, assigned by its producer.
notes.explanation: A standard remote ID aircraft may use a session ID instead; a module may not.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Instead of the control station's position, which location does a broadcast module transmit?
notes.back: The take-off location: its latitude, longitude and geometric altitude.
notes.explanation: The module must be able to work out the take-off location itself.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Besides its identity and the take-off location, what does a broadcast module transmit?
notes.back: The aircraft's latitude, longitude and geometric altitude, its velocity, and a UTC time mark.
notes.explanation: Unlike standard remote ID, a module sends no emergency status.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: A remote ID receiver shows a serial number, a drone's position and velocity, a time mark and the spot the drone took off from, but no pilot position. Which kind of remote ID is it?
notes.back: A broadcast module.
notes.explanation: Take-off location instead of control station position is the mark of a broadcast module.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: When flying with a broadcast module, what visual requirement applies?
notes.back: The person manipulating the flight controls must be able to see the aircraft at all times.
notes.explanation: This applies throughout the operation; the same condition applies in a FRIA.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Before takeoff with a broadcast module, what must the person manipulating the controls check?
notes.back: That the broadcast module is functioning.
notes.explanation: The module also tests itself before take-off and reports the result.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: For a drone flown with a broadcast module, which serial number must be on its Certificate of Aircraft Registration?
notes.back: The broadcast module's serial number.
notes.explanation: A serial number may be on only one Certificate of Aircraft Registration at a time.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 89.115(a)(1)(ii) (eCFR); § 48.110(a)(7); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.17.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: You want to move your broadcast module from drone A to drone B, both flown under part 107. What must you do before flying B?
notes.back: Move the module's serial number from drone A's registration certificate to drone B's.
notes.explanation: The serial number can be listed on only one Certificate of Aircraft Registration at a time.
notes.source: FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.17.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · AC 107-2A (2021), current on that date

notes.front: You fly a drone with a broadcast module behind a hill, out of your sight, for two minutes. Compliant with remote ID?
notes.back: No: with a broadcast module you must be able to see the aircraft at all times.
notes.explanation: Broadcasting from the module does not remove the need to keep the aircraft in sight.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Who may apply to establish a FRIA?
notes.back: Only community-based organizations recognized by the FAA, and educational institutions.
notes.explanation: Educational institutions include schools, trade schools, colleges and universities.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: What two conditions apply to flying without remote ID equipment at a FRIA?
notes.back: Aircraft and pilot stay within the FRIA's boundaries throughout, and the pilot can see the aircraft at all times.
notes.explanation: Any type of operation may use a FRIA, including part 107.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 89.115(b) (eCFR); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.17.3.2
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: You fly a drone with no remote ID equipment from inside a FRIA, and it drifts beyond the FRIA's boundary. Compliant?
notes.back: No: the aircraft and pilot must stay within the FRIA's boundaries throughout.
notes.explanation: Outside the FRIA the aircraft needs standard remote ID or a broadcast module.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: A drone-racing company wants its private track made a FRIA. Can it apply?
notes.back: No: only FAA-recognized community-based organizations and educational institutions may apply.
notes.explanation: A commercial company is neither.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: How long does an approved FRIA last?
notes.back: 48 calendar months; renewal must be requested at least 120 days before it expires.
notes.explanation: The FAA may refuse late requests, and can terminate a FRIA early, for example over a safety risk.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: When may the FAA authorise a flight without remote ID under § 89.120?
notes.back: When it is solely for aeronautical research or to show compliance with regulations.
notes.explanation: This is the only exception in § 89.105 besides general FAA authorisation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Can ADS-B Out equipment be used to comply with remote ID?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Remote ID must come from standard remote ID, a broadcast module or a FRIA.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: May a small UAS operated under part 107 fly with ADS-B Out in transmit mode?
notes.back: No, unless the FAA authorises it.
notes.explanation: ADS-B serves air traffic control and equipped aircraft; the ban holds unless the FAA authorises otherwise.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.53 Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out prohibition (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A pilot fits an ADS-B Out transmitter to his part 107 drone "to meet remote ID". What is wrong?
notes.back: Two things: ADS-B Out cannot meet remote ID, and part 107 bars transmitting it without FAA authorisation.
notes.explanation: He needs a standard remote ID aircraft, a broadcast module or a FRIA instead.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Before flying a foreign-registered civil drone with remote ID in the United States, what must you do?
notes.back: Submit a notice of identification to the FAA and obtain a Confirmation of Identification.
notes.explanation: The notice includes the operator's details, the aircraft's make, model and serial number, and its country and registration number.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Where must a Confirmation of Identification be kept during flights?
notes.back: At the unmanned aircraft's control station, ready to show the FAA or a law enforcement officer.
notes.explanation: It does not count as U.S. aircraft registration.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: How accurate must the reported position of a standard remote ID aircraft and its control station be?
notes.back: Within 100 feet of the true position, with 95% probability.
notes.explanation: Broadcast modules must meet the same 100 ft standard for the aircraft and the take-off location.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: How accurate must the reported geometric altitudes be for a standard remote ID aircraft?
notes.back: Aircraft: within 150 feet. Control station: within 15 feet. Both with 95% probability.
notes.explanation: One way to remember it: the control station is on the ground near the pilot, so its limit is ten times tighter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: What timing standards apply to a remote ID broadcast?
notes.back: Position sent no later than 1.0 second after measurement, and at least 1 message per second.
notes.explanation: These apply to both standard remote ID aircraft and broadcast modules.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: What happens if a standard remote ID aircraft's remote ID is not working at takeoff?
notes.back: It must not be able to take off.
notes.explanation: It tests itself before takeoff, tells the pilot the result, and keeps monitoring until shutdown.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: What label must a newly produced standard remote ID aircraft or broadcast module carry?
notes.back: One showing it meets part 89: in English, legible, prominent and permanently affixed.
notes.explanation: This is the producer's duty under part 89's design and production rules.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Do part 89's design and production rules apply to a home-built drone?
notes.back: No, unless it is designed and produced to be a standard remote ID aircraft.
notes.explanation: Part 89 defines home-built as built by an individual solely for education or recreation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Besides home-built drones, which three kinds of unmanned aircraft are outside part 89's design and production rules?
notes.back: U.S. Government aircraft, aircraft of 0.55 lb or less, and aircraft built only for aeronautical research or compliance testing.
notes.explanation: Again, this does not apply to any built to be standard remote ID aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: Which second location does each broadcast: a standard remote ID aircraft and a broadcast module?
notes.back: Standard remote ID: the control station. Broadcast module: the take-off location. Both also broadcast the aircraft's own position.
notes.explanation: Only standard remote ID also sends an emergency status.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: A 0.5 lb home-built drone is outside part 89's design rules. Must it still meet remote ID when flown under part 107?
notes.back: Yes. The design exceptions cover how it is built, not how it is flown: use a broadcast module or a FRIA.
notes.explanation: Remote ID applies to operating any aircraft required to be registered, and part 107 requires registration.
notes.source: 14 CFR §§ 89.101, 89.105, 89.501(c) (eCFR); FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.17.1
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date

notes.front: How does remote ID differ from the registration marking on a drone?
notes.back: The unique identifier is a number displayed on the aircraft; remote ID broadcasts identity and location by radio during flight.
notes.explanation: Both are required for part 107 flying, and remote ID serial numbers are tied to the registration.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 89 as of that date
